pinterest.title: Coverage Hours, Second Shooters and Albums: What Moves a Wedding Photographer's Quote
pinterest.description: A photographer's quote is a sum of decisions, most of them yours. Hours of coverage, a second shooter who covers what one person physically can't, travel, an engagement session, albums, editing and delivery timing, and how the images may be used all change it. Sketch your day first, share the timeline with every photographer, and ask how overtime is charged if the evening runs late. Read the full guide.

pinterest.title: Booking a Destination Wedding Photographer: Questions to Settle in Writing
pinterest.description: A wedding abroad changes a photographer's quote. Settle who books and pays for flights and transfers, the currency of the quote, where the photographer stays, which events are covered across the weekend, venue rules on flash and drones, permits for beaches, piazzas or heritage sites, and who replaces the photographer if a flight is cancelled. Read the full guide.

slides: What actually shapes a wedding photographer's quote, and what a package should spell out in writing.
Read the coverage line first. Two quotes that look alike can hide very different hours.
One photographer or a team? A second shooter covers what one person physically can't: both sets of preparations, guests' faces during the vows, the room while you are outside for portraits.

A clear package states coverage, people, any pre-wedding session, the online gallery, edited images, delivery dates, album details, usage and copyright, and a backup plan. If it isn't written down, treat it as not included.
Ask about the extras: overtime, additional events, travel and accommodation, permits, album upgrades, rush editing and raw files.

In Australia, under the Copyright Act, a couple who commissions and pays for wedding photos for a private or domestic purpose owns the copyright by default. The agreement can exclude or modify that rule, so read the usage clause before you sign.
Compare quotes line by line: hours, people, deliverables, timing, rights, extras and terms. Only then look at the totals.

instagram_carousel.caption:
A single average says very little about the quote you will receive for a wedding like yours. It blends a short registry signing with a celebration over several days abroad, one photographer with a full team, a digital gallery with a hand-bound album.

Our new guide explains what actually shapes a wedding photographer's quote, what a package should spell out in writing, and what tends to sit outside it.

Before you ask for quotes:
- Sketch the day: getting ready, the ceremony, portraits, the reception and the moment you want the camera to stop.
- Send every photographer the same written brief: date, venue, guest numbers, timeline, events and the products you want.
- Ask who exactly will photograph your wedding, and whether their name is in the contract.
- Ask how many edited images to expect, and the date the full gallery will be delivered. Get that date in writing.

Where you stand in Australia:
- Under the consumer guarantees, a photographer must use an acceptable level of care and skill, and those basic rights can't be taken away by anything the business says or does.
- Under the Copyright Act, a couple who commissions and pays for wedding photos for a private or domestic purpose owns the copyright by default, but the agreement can exclude or modify that rule.
This is general information, not legal advice, so read the usage and copyright clause before you sign.

A lower headline price with fewer hours and a slower delivery date is a different product, not a saving. Decide which images matter most, and protect those hours first.
